claim: Insects have been traditionally thought to be entirely dependent on their innate immune system with little capacity for acquisition of experience from previous infections.
source: Traditionally, insects have been thought to be entirely dependent on their innate immune system, which has little capacity for the acquisition of experience from previous infections.
evidence: This represents a historical scientific perspective that is being challenged in the manuscript.

claim: Experimental evidence has shown that insects can develop long-term, pathogen-specific immune memory.
source: However, much experimental evidence has challenged this view, showing that insects can develop long-term, pathogen-specific immune memory, which in some cases can be transmitted to offspring.
evidence: The manuscript references experimental evidence throughout that demonstrates this capability.

claim: Insect immune memory can be transmitted to offspring in some cases.
source: However, much experimental evidence has challenged this view, showing that insects can develop long-term, pathogen-specific immune memory, which in some cases can be transmitted to offspring.
evidence: The manuscript discusses transgenerational immune priming with experimental examples.

claim: The mechanism underlying insect immune memory is not fully understood.
source: Although significant progress has been made in this area, the underlying mechanism is still not fully understood, and a number of fundamental questions remain unanswered.
evidence: The authors acknowledge gaps in current understanding throughout the review.

claim: Individual immune mechanisms have evolved over millions of years of coevolution between the host's immune system and pathogens.
source: Individual immune mechanisms have evolved over millions of years of coevolution between the host's immune system and the pathogens attempting to evade it (Müller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Müller et al., 2018.

claim: Acquisition of experience from initial contact with a pathogen represents a crucial advantage for hosts that can gain resistance to reinfections.
source: Acquisition of experience from the initial contact with the pathogen, therefore, represents the crucial advantage for hosts that can gain resistance to reinfections (Palmieri et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palmieri et al., 2021.

claim: Organisms can gain immune experience at both systemic and cell-autonomous levels.
source: In nature, we can observe various sophisticated strategies that allow organisms to gain a certain degree of immune experience at both the systemic and cell-autonomous levels (Divangahi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Divangahi et al., 2021.

claim: The term 'acquired immunity' was previously used almost exclusively to refer to adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates.
source: While the term 'acquired immunity' was previously used almost exclusively to refer to adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates, it is now applied more broadly to encompass various forms of acquired immune experience (Little et al., 2005; Rimer et al., 2014; Cooper and Eleftherianos, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Little et al., 2005; Rimer et al., 2014; Cooper and Eleftherianos, 2017.

claim: Three basic categories of acquired immune responses are distinguished: immune priming, immune training, and immune memory.
source: Currently, three basic categories of acquired immune responses (immune priming, immune training, and immune memory; Box 1) are distinguished according to the character and specificity of the initial immune response (Tang et al., 2023; Vuscan et al., 2024; Netea et al., 2019; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The belief that only vertebrates with adaptive immune systems can form specific and long-lasting immune memory is incorrect.
source: The original anthropocentric belief that only vertebrates with adaptive immune systems can form specific and long-lasting immune memory is incorrect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complex mechanisms underlying the adaptability of immune response exist in prokaryotic bacteria and archaea.
source: Advances over the last two decades in comparative and evolutionary immunology have revealed complex mechanisms underlying the adaptability of immune response in prokaryotic bacteria and archaea, and various degrees of acquired immunity can be observed in almost all eukaryotes (Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022.

claim: Various degrees of acquired immunity can be observed in almost all eukaryotes.
source: Advances over the last two decades in comparative and evolutionary immunology have revealed complex mechanisms underlying the adaptability of immune response in prokaryotic bacteria and archaea, and various degrees of acquired immunity can be observed in almost all eukaryotes (Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Newsom et al., 2020; Bagasra and Prilliman, 2004; Gomes et al., 2022.

claim: Immune priming is characterized by persistent activation of the immune system following the first immune challenge, resulting in an enhanced immune response to the second challenge.
source: Immune priming is characterized by the persistent activation of the immune system following the first immune challenge, resulting in an enhanced immune response to the second challenge.
evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Immune training and immune memory are biphasic, meaning immune response returns to baseline before the second challenge.
source: In contrast, immune training and immune memory are biphasic, meaning immune response returns to baseline before the second challenge.
evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses.
source: While immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses, immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner, i.e., the same pathogen must be involved in both the first and second challenges (homologous infection; solid line).
evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner requiring the same pathogen in both challenges.
source: While immune priming and immune training are pathogen-nonspecific responses, immune memory operates in a pathogen-specific manner, i.e., the same pathogen must be involved in both the first and second challenges (homologous infection; solid line).
evidence: Defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: More than 150 distinct prokaryotic immune mechanisms have been identified through whole-genome sequencing and comparative analysis.
source: Whole-genome sequencing and comparative analysis of hundreds of prokaryotic organisms have led to the discovery of genomic islands that accumulate immune-related genes, enabling the identification of more than 150 distinct prokaryotic immune mechanisms (Bernheim et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernheim et al., 2024.

claim: Many prokaryotic immune mechanisms are present to some extent in eukaryotes.
source: Notably, many of these mechanisms are also present to some extent in eukaryotes, indicating that particularly cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life (Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023.

claim: Cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life.
source: Notably, many of these mechanisms are also present to some extent in eukaryotes, indicating that particularly cell-autonomous immune mechanisms are remarkably conserved across the tree of life (Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayo-Muñoz et al., 2023.

claim: Immune mechanisms that evolved in prokaryotes as protection against mobile genetic elements and pathogens were later adopted and repurposed by eukaryotic immune systems.
source: The prevailing hypothesis for this phenomenon is that immune mechanisms that evolved during the rapid evolution of prokaryotes, as protection against mobile genetic elements and other pathogens, were later adopted and repurposed by eukaryotic immune systems.
evidence: This is presented as a prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: Acquisition of immune traits likely occurred through horizontal gene transfer mediated by retrotransposons.
source: The acquisition of these immune traits likely occurred through horizontal gene transfer mediated by retrotransposons, highlighting the central role of domesticated mobile genetic elements in the evolution of the eukaryotic immune system (Wein and Sorek, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wein and Sorek, 2022.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria.
source: This system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria, where it serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages (Rath et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rath et al., 2015.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas system serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages in prokaryotes.
source: This system is widely present in most archaea and many bacteria, where it serves as a defense mechanism against bacteriophages (Rath et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rath et al., 2015.

claim: Bacteria and archaea can recognize foreign nucleic acids, cleave them into smaller fragments, and integrate these fragments into their own genome during bacteriophage infection.
source: When a bacterium or archaeon is infected by a bacteriophage, it can recognize the foreign nucleic acids, cleave them into smaller fragments, and integrate these fragments into its own genome.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: Viral DNA fragments are inserted into a specific region of the host genome known as CRISPR, which acts as a repository of previous viral encounters.
source: Viral DNA fragments are inserted into a specific region of the host genome known as CRISPR, which acts as a repository of previous viral encounters (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: Upon subsequent viral infection, the CRISPR locus is transcribed, producing CRISPR-pre-mRNA, which is then cleaved into individual CRISPR RNAs.
source: Upon subsequent viral infection, the CRISPR locus is transcribed, producing CRISPR-pre-mRNA, which is then cleaved into individual CRISPR RNAs.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: Short RNA fragments from CRISPR guide Cas nucleases to perform sequence-specific cleavage of viral genetic material.
source: These short RNA fragments guide Cas nucleases to perform sequence-specific cleavage of viral genetic material (Hille et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hille et al., 2018.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas system is regarded as a clear example of adaptive immunity in prokaryotes.
source: This sophisticated mechanism is widely regarded as a clear example of adaptive immunity since the integration of viral sequences into the host genome serves as a form of immune memory, while sequence-specific cleavage ensures the specificity of the immune response (Jiang and Doudna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang and Doudna, 2017.

claim: Key enzymes that protect prokaryotes from mobile genetic elements are co-opted transposases derived from retrotransposons.
source: Interestingly, key enzymes that protect prokaryotes from mobile genetic elements are co-opted transposases derived from retrotransposons (Koonin and Krupovic, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koonin and Krupovic, 2015.

claim: Enzymes responsible for somatic recombination (Rag1 and Rag2) in T and B lymphocytes are derived from the Transib family of retrotransposons.
source: A similar phenomenon is observed in the adaptive immune system of jawed vertebrates, where the enzymes responsible for somatic recombination (Rag1 and Rag2) in T and B lymphocytes are derived from the Transib family of retrotransposons (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2016.

claim: Endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the insect genome.
source: Another example, which will be discussed in detail later in this review, is the adaptive antiviral immunity in insects. In this system, endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the genome, thus creating a long-lasting and heritable immune memory (Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017.

claim: Integration of viral nucleic acids into the insect genome creates a long-lasting and heritable immune memory.
source: In this system, endogenous transposons Ty1 and Ty3 play a central role in acquiring copies of viral nucleic acids and integrating them into the genome, thus creating a long-lasting and heritable immune memory (Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017.

claim: There are intriguing parallels in the convergent evolution of mechanisms of acquired immunity.
source: These examples reveal intriguing parallels in the convergent evolution of mechanisms of acquired immunity (Eaglesham and Kranzusch, 2024), all of which exploit the enzymatic activities of genes acquired from domesticated retrotransposons to establish immune memory by modifying host genomic information.
evidence: Supported by citation to Eaglesham and Kranzusch, 2024.

claim: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth.
source: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth (Stork, 2018), and like other animals, they are exposed to a wide range of pathogens throughout their lifetimes, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids (Federici, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stork, 2018.

claim: Insects are exposed to a wide range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids.
source: Insects are the most abundant group of animals on Earth (Stork, 2018), and like other animals, they are exposed to a wide range of pathogens throughout their lifetimes, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and parasitoids (Federici, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Federici, 2009.

claim: Insects can act as reservoirs for pathogens, serving as vectors that facilitate their amplification and transmission, including to humans.
source: In such cases, insects can act as reservoirs for these pathogens, serving as vectors that facilitate their amplification and transmission, including to humans (St Leger, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to St Leger, 2021.

claim: The cuticle acts as a physical barrier in insects, offering strong protection against most pathogens in the environment.
source: In insects, the primary immune defense is provided by the cuticle, which acts as a physical barrier, offering strong protection against most pathogens in the environment.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The most common routes of infection in insects are through wounds, the digestive system, or the tracheal system.
source: Consequently, the most common routes of infection are through wounds, the digestive system, or the tracheal system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect infection routes.

claim: Once the cuticle is breached, immune cells are activated, triggering both cellular and humoral immune responses.
source: Once the cuticle is breached, immune cells are activated, triggering both cellular and humoral immune responses (Buchon et al., 2014; Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buchon et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The insect innate immune system is largely based on evolutionarily conserved pathways that are also found in mammals.
source: The insect innate immune system is largely based on evolutionarily conserved pathways, which are also found, to some extent, in mammals.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in comparative immunology.

claim: The cellular branch of insect immunity includes various effector immune cells known as hemocytes.
source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Plasmatocytes perform phagocytosis during the immune response.
source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Lamellocytes perform encapsulation during the immune response.
source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Crystal cells activate phenoloxidases during the immune response.
source: The cellular branch includes various effector immune cells, known as hemocytes, which perform distinct functions during the immune response, such as phagocytosis (plasmatocytes), encapsulation (lamellocytes), activation of phenoloxidases (crystal cells), degranulation (granulocytes), or the release of extracellular traps (Mahanta et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanta et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Some insect species possess specialized immune cell types including spherulocytes, oenocytoids, coagulocytes, adipohemocytes, and thrombocytoids.
source: In addition, some insect species possess specialized immune cell types, such as spherulocytes, oenocytoids, coagulocytes, adipohemocytes, and thrombocytoids, which further contribute to pathogen elimination, wound healing, metabolic homeostasis, as well as nutrient transport (Eleftherianos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eleftherianos et al., 2021.

claim: Extracellular traps are composed of double-stranded DNA, histones, elastase, and myeloperoxidase.
source: These extracellular web-like structures, composed of double-stranded DNA, histones, elastase, and myeloperoxidase, serve to trap, immobilize, and kill pathogens (Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nascimento et al., 2018.

claim: Key signaling pathways and transcription factors involved in phagocytosis, hematopoiesis, cell proliferation, and differentiation have remained conserved for over 550 million years of evolution.
source: Although insect immune cell types and their functions are less diverse than those in vertebrates, the key signaling pathways and transcription factors involved in phagocytosis (Melcarne et al., 2019), hematopoiesis (Banerjee et al., 2019), cell proliferation, and differentiation (Evans et al., 2003) have remained conserved for over 550 million years of evolution.
evidence: Supported by citations to Melcarne et al., 2019; Banerjee et al., 2019; Evans et al., 2003.

claim: Pathogen recognition receptors can be classified into several groups including NOD-like receptors, C-type lectins, thioester-containing proteins, scavenger receptors, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, Toll-like receptors, and Gram-negative-binding proteins.
source: Pathogens are detected by pathogen recognition receptors that can be classified into several groups, such as NOD-like receptors, C-type lectins, thioester-containing proteins, scavenger receptors, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, Toll-like receptors, or Gram-negative-binding proteins.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect immune recognition.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway.
source: While Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway, Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway (Browne et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2013.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway.
source: While Gram-positive bacteria and fungi predominately activate the Toll pathway, Gram-negative bacteria induce the IMD signaling pathway (Browne et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2013.

claim: Insects utilize encapsulation and melanization when encountering foreign objects too large for phagocytosis.
source: When encountering foreign objects too large for phagocytosis, such as parasitoid eggs or nematodes, insects utilize encapsulation and melanization (Bilandžija et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bilandžija et al., 2017.

claim: Prophenoloxidases catalyze the conversion of phenylalanine and tyrosine into melanin, producing toxic free radical by-products.
source: These enzymes catalyze the conversion of the amino acids phenylalanine and tyrosine into melanin, producing toxic free radical by-products that help eliminate the pathogen (Tang, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang, 2009.

claim: The conserved intracellular immune response based on RNA interference (RNAi) is the most thoroughly studied antiviral mechanism in insects.
source: The conserved intracellular immune response based on RNA interference (RNAi) remains the most thoroughly studied antiviral mechanism in insects (Gammon and Mello, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gammon and Mello, 2015.

claim: Viral double-stranded RNA is cleaved by the endoribonuclease Dicer into short small interfering RNA (siRNA) fragments.
source: In this pathway, viral double-stranded RNA is cleaved by the endoribonuclease Dicer into short small interfering RNA (siRNA) fragments.
evidence: This describes the established RNAi mechanism.

claim: Dicer and Argonaut form the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which facilitates sequence-specific recognition and cleavage of viral nucleic acids.
source: Dicer, together with the RNA-dependent nuclease Argonaut, forms the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which facilitates the sequence-specific recognition and cleavage of viral nucleic acids (Leggewie and Schnettler, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leggewie and Schnettler, 2018.

claim: The cGAS-like receptor STING-Relish pathway plays a central role in general antiviral defense in Drosophila.
source: While the interferon response characteristic of mammalian species has not been identified in insects, recent findings suggest that the cGAS-like receptor STING-Relish pathway plays a central role in general antiviral defense in Drosophila.
evidence: This is based on recent findings in the field.

claim: STING signaling activates the IMD pathway transcription factor Relish to regulate the expression of genes potentially involved in antiviral defense.
source: Similarly, in insects, it has been documented that STING signaling activates the IMD pathway transcription factor Relish to regulate the expression of genes potentially involved in antiviral defense (Goto et al., 2018; Decout et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goto et al., 2018; Decout et al., 2021.

claim: Insect plasmatocytes undergo metabolic rewiring in response to acute bacterial infection, shifting from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis.
source: Similar to mammalian macrophages, insect plasmatocytes undergo a fundamental metabolic rewiring in response to acute bacterial infection, shifting their predominant ATP metabolic pathway from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis (Krejčová et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krejčová et al., 2019.

claim: Plasmatocytes secrete Imaginal morphogenesis protein late 2 to induce nutrient mobilization from the central metabolic organ.
source: To secure these resources, plasmatocytes secrete various factors, such as Imaginal morphogenesis protein late 2, to induce nutrient mobilization from the central metabolic organ while limiting their consumption by peripheral nonimmune tissues.
evidence: This is based on research findings described in the manuscript.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides are rapidly expressed by immune cells and the fat body during systemic infection.
source: During systemic infection, antimicrobial peptides are rapidly expressed by immune cells and the fat body (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides act as opsonizing factors, embedding themselves in the hydrophobic portion of bacterial or fungal membrane.
source: Due to their positive charge, these peptides act as opsonizing factors, embedding themselves in the hydrophobic portion of bacterial or fungal membrane. This facilitates recognition by immune cells, destabilizes the pathogen's membrane, and ultimately leads to cell death (Dho et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dho et al., 2023.

claim: Clotting proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminase, which is homologous to factor XIIIa in vertebrates.
source: These molecules are cross-linked by transglutaminase, which is homologous to factor XIIIa, a key component of the vertebrate coagulation cascade.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect clotting mechanisms.

claim: The ability of the insect immune system to develop acquired immunity has been documented in a wide range of species.
source: The ability of the insect immune system to develop some form of acquired immunity has been documented in a wide range of species (Cooper and Eleftherianos, 2017; Kurtz and Franz, 2003; Trauer-Kizilelma and Hilker, 2015; Freitak et al., 2009; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Flies inoculated with an avirulent strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa mount increased resistance to a highly virulent strain.
source: In this study, the authors demonstrated that flies that were first inoculated with an avirulent strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa mount an increased resistance to a highly virulent strain.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from a cited study.

claim: Flies primed with either a sublethal dose or heat-killed Streptococcus pneumoniae were protected against a lethal challenge of the same bacterium administered 7 days later.
source: Flies primed with either a sublethal dose or heat-killed Streptococcus pneumoniae were protected against a lethal challenge of the same bacterium administered 7 days later, allowing sufficient time for pathogen clearance.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from Pham et al., 2007.

claim: Administration of a sublethal dose of Beauveria bassiana provided protection against a subsequent lethal dose of the same fungus.
source: A similar effect was achieved by administering a sublethal dose of the natural fungal pathogen Beauveria bassiana, which provided protection against a subsequent lethal dose of the same fungus.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from Pham et al., 2007.

claim: A remarkably high degree of specificity of immune memory has been documented in Tribolium castaneum, whose immune system can discriminate between closely related bacterial strains of Bacillus thuringiensis.
source: A remarkably high degree of specificity of immune memory has been documented in Tribolium castaneum, whose immune system can discriminate between closely related bacterial strains of Bacillus thuringiensis (Roth et al., 2009; Futo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roth et al., 2009; Futo et al., 2017.

claim: Immune memory in bumblebees lasts for several weeks after clearance of bacteria from the first exposure.
source: Narrow specificity and increased protection have also been observed in the bumblebee, Bombus terrestris, where the immune memory lasts for several weeks after clearance of bacteria from the first exposure (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2006.

claim: Adult flies orally infected with Drosophila C virus during the larval stage exhibited increased tolerance to subsequent reinfections with the same virus.
source: Mondotte and colleagues conducted trans-stadial assays, revealing that adult flies orally infected with Drosophila C virus during the larval stage exhibited increased tolerance to subsequent reinfections with the same virus.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from Mondotte et al., 2018.

claim: Trans-stadial acquired immunity has been documented in Aedes aegypti, where infection of larvae with inactive dengue virus protects against subsequent infection in adult mosquitoes.
source: Trans-stadial acquired immunity has also been documented in Aedes aegypti, where infection of larvae with inactive dengue virus has been shown to protect against subsequent infection in adult mosquitoes (Vargas et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vargas et al., 2020.

claim: Larval exposure to Streptococcus pyogenes or E. coli led to increased longevity of adult Anopheles arabiensis females challenged with the respective pathogen.
source: Trans-stadial protection has also been documented in another mosquito, Anopheles arabiensis. In this study, larval exposure to Streptococcus pyogenes or E. coli led to increased longevity of adult females challenged with the respective pathogen (Patel and Oliver, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patel and Oliver, 2024.

claim: Adult Tribolium confusum beetles infested with Gregarina minuta display enhanced survival resistance when infected as larvae.
source: Indeed, this model has shown that adult beetles infested with G. minuta display enhanced survival resistance when infected as larvae, highlighting the persistence of immune protection across life stages (Thomas and Rudolf, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas and Rudolf, 2010.

claim: Transgenerational immune priming is likely to evolve in environments where offspring have a high probability of encountering the same pathogen as their parents.
source: Since mounting an immune response is connected with significant energy costs, TgIP is likely to evolve in environments where offspring have a high probability of encountering the same pathogen as their parents (Thomas and Rudolf, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas and Rudolf, 2010.

claim: Larvae of immunized honeybee queens display improved survival compared to larval progeny of nonimmunized queens when fed Paenibacillus larvae spores.
source: It has been shown that these individuals display improved survival compared to larval progeny of nonimmunized queens. This enhanced survival was presumably due to a threefold increase in the number of differential hemocytes (all hemocyte types except for prohemocytes) (Hernández López et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hernández López et al., 2014.

claim: When bumblebee queens were challenged with heat-killed Arthrobacter globiformis, both their eggs and progeny workers exhibited significantly higher antibacterial activity when injected by lipopolysaccharides.
source: When queens were challenged with heat-killed Arthrobacter globiformis, both their eggs and progeny workers exhibited significantly higher antibacterial activity when injected by lipopolysaccharides, compared to controls (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007.

claim: Transgenerational immune priming has been connected with certain costs, as individuals were more susceptible to a pathogen distinct from maternal challenge.
source: However, such TgIP has been connected with certain costs since these individuals were more susceptible to a pathogen distinct from maternal challenge, the trypanosome parasite Crithidia bombi (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007.

claim: Female offspring of immunized Manduca sexta parents laid fewer eggs than those derived from control parents.
source: The costs of TgIP have also been investigated in tobacco hornworm Manduca sexta, where female offspring of immunized parents laid fewer eggs than those derived from control parents (Trauer and Hilker, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trauer and Hilker, 2013.

claim: After parental exposure to heat-killed E. coli or B. thuringiensis, transgenerational immune priming occurs through fathers as well as mothers in Tribolium castaneum.
source: After parental exposure to heat-killed E. coli or B. thuringiensis, TgIP occurs through fathers as well as mothers (Roth et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roth et al., 2010.

claim: Offspring of Indian meal moth parents exposed to a low dose of their natural DNA virus during the larval stage were less susceptible to viral challenge.
source: Offspring of Indian meal moth (Plodia interpunctella) parents exposed to a low dose of their natural DNA virus during the larval stage were less susceptible to viral challenge (Tidbury et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tidbury et al., 2011.

claim: The offspring of immune-challenged parents inherit viral DNA and exhibit upregulation of genes related to chromatin and DNA binding.
source: Using D. melanogaster and A. aegypti as models, the authors revealed that the offspring of immune-challenged parents inherit viral DNA and exhibit upregulation of genes related to chromatin and DNA binding (Mondotte et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mondotte et al., 2020.

claim: Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with arboviruses can transmit specific immunity to their offspring.
source: Similar results were obtained in a recent study by Rodriguez-Andres and colleagues, who documented that A. aegypti mosquitoes infected with arboviruses can transmit specific immunity to their offspring (Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024.

claim: Alterations in the epigenetic landscape, specifically DNA methylation and histone acetylation, were detected in the F1 generation of parents fed non-pathogenic E. coli or Serratia entomophila.
source: Additionally, alterations in the epigenetic landscape, specifically DNA methylation and histone acetylation, were detected in the F1 generation of parents fed non-pathogenic E. coli or the entomopathogen Serratia entomophila (Gegner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gegner et al., 2019.

claim: Immune memory appears to persist through developmental stages and may be passed on to subsequent generations in insects.
source: Moreover, immune memory appears to persist through developmental stages and may even be passed on to subsequent generations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acquired immune memory can be divided into three phases: antigen acquisition, development of immune specificity, and maintenance of immune memory.
source: Acquired immune memory can be in general divided into three phases
evidence: This is a conceptual framework presented by the authors.

claim: Virus-infected cells activate the transcription factors Hop and Dome, leading to increased production of unpaired family cytokines.
source: Virus-infected cells commonly activate the transcription factors Hop and Dome, leading to increased production of unpaired family cytokines (Upd1, Upd2, Upd3).
evidence: This describes established mechanisms of insect antiviral immunity.

claim: Elevated levels of unpaired cytokines in circulation activate macrophage-like plasmatocytes via the JAK-STAT signaling pathway.
source: Elevated levels of these cytokines in circulation activate macrophage-like plasmatocytes via the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, attracting them to virus-infected tissues (Sabin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabin et al., 2010.

claim: The elimination of virus-infected apoptotic cells by activated plasmatocytes is crucial for viral resistance in Drosophila.
source: The elimination of virus-infected apoptotic cells by activated plasmatocytes has been shown to be crucial for viral resistance in Drosophila (Saleh et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saleh et al., 2009.

claim: The presence of viral double-stranded RNA in the phagolysosome leads to permeabilization of its membrane and acquisition of viral genetic information.
source: However, plasmatocytes do not simply degrade all engulfed material; the presence of viral double-stranded RNA in the phagolysosome leads to permeabilization of its membrane and acquisition of viral genetic information (Tanaka et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2024.

claim: Plasmatocytes use viral RNA as a template for reverse transcription, integrating fragments of complementary antisense viral DNA into their genomes.
source: Plasmatocytes then use viral RNA as a template for reverse transcription, integrating fragments of complementary antisense viral DNA into their genomes (Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tassetto et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Retrotransposon activity increases more than 20-fold in plasmatocytes upon viral infection.
source: Nevertheless, retrotransposon activity increases more than 20-fold in plasmatocytes upon viral infection, and mere inhibition of retrotransposons completely abolishes the host's resistance to infection.
evidence: This describes experimental findings on retrotransposon activity.

claim: Virus-derived DNA is commonly flanked by sequences from Ty2 and Ty3 retrotransposons of the LTR family.
source: Sequencing of circular DNA from infected plasmatocytes reveals that virus-derived DNA is commonly flanked by sequences from Ty2 and Ty3 retrotransposons of the LTR family (Roy et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roy et al., 2020.

claim: Viral RNA integrated into the host genome as endogenous viral element serves as a template for producing secondary viral DNAs.
source: Viral RNA, integrated into specific regions of the host genome as endogenous viral element (EVE), serves as a template for producing secondary viral DNAs (svDNAs) (Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tassetto et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of secondary viral DNAs provides cells with cell-autonomous resistance to viral infection by priming the activation of Dicer and Argonaute proteins.
source: Expression of svDNAs subsequently provides cells with cell-autonomous resistance to viral infection as it primes the activation of Dicer and Argonaute proteins, which together form the RISC that governs sequence-specific elimination of viral RNA (van Rij et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Rij et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Plasmatocytes disseminate secondary viral DNA systemically, enclosed within extracellular vesicles or via tunneling nanotubes.
source: Additionally, plasmatocytes disseminate svDNA systemically, enclosed within extracellular vesicles or via tunneling nanotubes, along with activating cytokine signaling (Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tassetto et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Plasmatocytes can amplify viral DNA and spread it as prophylaxis to other cells, enabling them to acquire resistance against specific viruses.
source: Thus, plasmatocytes, even without being infected themselves, can amplify viral DNA and spread it as a form of prophylaxis to other cells, enabling them to acquire resistance against specific viruses (Mondotte et al., 2020; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mondotte et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Insect antiviral immune memory is based on the integration of viral sequences into the genome, which is later used for sequence-specific elimination of viral nucleic acids.
source: Similar to the CRISPR-Cas system, insect antiviral immune memory is based on the integration of viral sequences into the genome, which is later used for sequence-specific elimination of viral nucleic acids.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the evidence presented.

claim: The integration of viral DNA into the host genome provides insects with transgenerational adaptive immunity.
source: Notably, the integration of viral DNA into the host genome also provides insects with transgenerational adaptive immunity (Mondotte et al., 2020; Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mondotte et al., 2020; Rodriguez-Andres et al., 2024.

claim: Analogous antiviral immune memory mechanisms occur in ants, beetles, aphids, butterflies, mosquitoes, flies, and ticks.
source: Comparisons of small RNAs produced from EVE regions in different insect species indicate that analogous mechanisms likely occur in ants (Hymenoptera), beetles (Coleoptera), aphids (Hemiptera), butterflies (Lepidoptera), mosquitoes and flies (Diptera), and even ticks (Ixodida, Arachnida, Chelicerata) (Gilbert and Belliardo, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert and Belliardo, 2022.

claim: An analogous antiviral immune memory mechanism has been identified in crustaceans.
source: Recently, an analogous mechanism has also been identified in crustaceans, suggesting that the mechanism of antiviral immune memory may be common across most arthropods (Taengchaiyaphum et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taengchaiyaphum et al., 2021.

claim: EVE transcription gives rise to both siRNA and longer transcripts known as Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) in some species.
source: In some of these species, EVE transcription gives rise not only to siRNA but also to longer transcripts known as Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs).
evidence: This describes variations in the antiviral immune mechanism.

claim: piRNAs bind to RISC complex proteins, Piwi (PIWI) and Aubergine (AUB), and enter the secondary piRNA biogenesis pathway in the cytosol.
source: piRNAs bind to RISC complex proteins, Piwi (PIWI) and Aubergine (AUB), and enter the secondary piRNA biogenesis pathway in the cytosol, also known as the 'ping-pong' pathway (Tassetto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tassetto et al., 2019 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Studies have documented that in mice viral infections are accompanied by the systemic spread of virus-derived small interfering RNAs via extracellular vesicles.
source: Studies have documented that in mice viral infections are accompanied by the systemic spread of virus-derived small interfering RNAs via extracellular vesicles, which provide recipient cells with acquired resistance to subsequent viral infections (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: Contradictory findings in mammals suggest that Dicer exhibits negligible enzymatic activity in virus-infected cells.
source: However, contradictory findings in mammals suggest that Dicer exhibits negligible enzymatic activity in virus-infected cells, and its knockdown does not substantially affect viral load (Berkhout, 2018; Wang and Li, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berkhout, 2018; Wang and Li, 2024.

claim: Insects lack the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and tapasin (Tap) genes, essential for canonical antigen presentation in mammals.
source: Although insects lack the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and tapasin (Tap) genes, essential for canonical antigen presentation in mammals, certain evidence suggests that other components of the antigen processing machinery may be conserved.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect immune systems.

claim: Expressing MHC and tapasin genes heterologously in Drosophila S2 cells enables them to present antigens on their surface.
source: This is demonstrated by the fact that simply expressing these two genes heterogously in Drosophila S2 cells, derived from embryonic macrophages-like cells, enables them to present antigens on their surface (Ortmann et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ortmann et al., 1997.

claim: Mammalian macrophages disseminate antigens via extracellular vesicles, encapsulated within multilamellar bodies, or through eruptophagy.
source: Recent studies in mice have shown that mammalian macrophages disseminate antigens via extracellular vesicles, encapsulated within multilamellar bodies, or through a process known as eruptophagy, where the phagolysosome's contents are released directly into the extracellular space (Smith et al., 2017; El Safadi et al., 2024; Lindenbergh and Stoorvogel, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2017; El Safadi et al., 2024; Lindenbergh and Stoorvogel, 2018.

claim: Circulating bacterial antigens have been found in complexes with hemolymph proteins such as lipoproteins, vitellogenins, and storage proteins in insects.
source: This idea aligns with numerous observations in insects, where circulating bacterial antigens have been found in complexes with hemolymph proteins such as lipoproteins, vitellogenins, and several storage proteins (Salmela et al., 2015; Kato et al., 1994; Kanost and Zhao, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salmela et al., 2015; Kato et al., 1994; Kanost and Zhao, 1996.

claim: Dscam consists of extracellular, transmembrane, and cytosolic regions.
source: Dscam consists of extracellular, transmembrane, and cytosolic regions.
evidence: This describes the structure of Dscam, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The extracellular part of Dscam contains 10 immunoglobulin domains and 6 fibronectin type III repeats.
source: The extracellular part of Dscam contains 10 immunoglobulin domains and 6 fibronectin type III repeats (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Three immunoglobulin domains of Dscam (2, 3, and 7) are encoded by multivariant exons (4, 6, and 9), which in Drosophila have 12, 48, and 33 alternative variants, respectively.
source: Three of the immunoglobulin domains (2, 3, and 7) are encoded by multivariant exons (4, 6, and 9), which, in Drosophila, have 12, 48, and 33 alternative variants, respectively (Wojtowicz et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wojtowicz et al., 2007 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Individual DSCAM variants are produced through mutually exclusive alternative splicing.
source: Individual DSCAM variants are produced through mutually exclusive alternative splicing, which ensures that only one variant from each multivariant exon is included in the final mRNA (Graveley, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graveley, 2005 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Dscam can generate up to 19,008 immunoglobulin domain variants.
source: Consequently, Dscam can generate up to 19,008 (12 × 48 × 33) immunoglobulin domain variants, with additional variability arising from alternative splicing of exon 17, producing either membrane-bound or secreted forms (Celotto and Graveley, 2001; Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by citation to Celotto and Graveley, 2001 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Drosophila Dscam is the gene with the highest number of alternative transcripts in animals.
source: Drosophila Dscam is the gene with the highest number of alternative transcripts in animals, drawing significant scientific attention to the mechanisms regulating such a complex process.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Dscam.

claim: Inclusion of a single variant from a multivariant exon is achieved through the pairing of a 'docking sequence' with a 'selector sequence'.
source: Inclusion of a single variant from a multivariant exon is achieved through the pairing of a 'docking sequence' at the end of the previous exon with a 'selector sequence' preceding each variant in the specific multivariable exon (Graveley, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graveley, 2005 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: More than twelve RNA-binding proteins are involved in Dscam alternative splicing in S2 cells.
source: Moreover, it seems that each of the three multivariant exons shows specific characteristics in the alternative splicing mechanism (Ustaoglu et al., 2019; McManus and Graveley, 2011), which aligns with recent identification of more than twelve RNA-binding proteins involved in Dscam alternative splicing in S2 cells (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: Alternative exon skipping and selection of alternative splicing sites for exons 18 and 23 generate eight different variants of Dscam cytosolic tail.
source: It has been reported that alternative exon skipping and selection of alternative splicing sites for exons 18 and 23 generate eight different variants of Dscam cytosolic tail.
evidence: This describes reported findings on Dscam structure.

claim: Dscam plays a dual role in insects: immune response and development of the central nervous system.
source: Dscam plays a dual role in insects; in addition to its function in immune response, it is essential for the development of the central nervous system (CNS) (Schmucker et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmucker et al., 2000.

claim: The combination of several Dscam splicing variants provides each neuron in the Drosophila CNS with a unique recognition code.
source: The combination of several Dscam splicing variants provides each neuron in the Drosophila CNS with a unique recognition code (Hattori et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hattori et al., 2007.

claim: Each DSCAM variant can form homodimeric bonds with another DSCAM molecule containing identical domains.
source: Each DSCAM variant can form homodimeric bonds with another DSCAM molecule containing identical domains, allowing neurons to recognize their own cellular surfaces.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of DSCAM function in neurons.

claim: Homodimeric interaction of DSCAM triggers intracellular signaling, leading to remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton and repulsion of cellular extensions.
source: This homodimeric interaction triggers intracellular signaling, leading to the remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton and repulsion of cellular extensions (Wojtowicz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wojtowicz et al., 2004.

claim: Dscam is highly expressed in Drosophila plasmatocytes during bacterial infection.
source: It has been shown that Dscam is highly expressed in Drosophila plasmatocytes during bacterial infection (Celotto and Graveley, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Celotto and Graveley, 2001.

claim: Both circulating and membrane-bound forms of DSCAM are produced by plasmatocytes, facilitating the opsonization and phagocytosis of pathogens.
source: Both circulating and membrane-bound forms of DSCAM are produced by plasmatocytes, facilitating the opsonization and phagocytosis of pathogens (Watson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Watson et al., 2005.

claim: The binding of DSCAM to a pathogen alters its tertiary structure, allowing it to be recognized by membrane-bound DSCAM.
source: It is believed that the binding of DSCAM to a pathogen alters its tertiary structure, allowing it to be recognized by membrane-bound DSCAM, which facilitates internalization through phagocytosis (Dong et al., 2006; Wan et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2006; Wan et al., 2023.

claim: Both circulating and membrane-bound forms of DSCAM are necessary for combating bacterial infections.
source: However, both circulating and membrane-bound forms of DSCAM are necessary for combating bacterial infections (Li, 2021; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li, 2021; Li et al., 2019.

claim: During immune responses, Dscam undergoes alternative splicing, enabling plasmatocytes to produce nearly the full spectrum of DSCAM variants.
source: During immune responses, Dscam undergoes alternative splicing, enabling plasmatocytes to produce nearly the full spectrum of DSCAM variants.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Dscam diversification during immune responses.

claim: Infection by a specific pathogen results in the selection of specific Dscam variants that exhibit particularly high affinity for the pathogen's surface antigens.
source: However, this alternative splicing is not a random process in plasmatocytes. Infection by a specific pathogen results in the selection of specific Dscam variants that exhibit particularly high affinity for the pathogen's surface antigens (Meijers et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meijers et al., 2007.

claim: Activation of macrophage-like hemocytes in the Chinese mitten crab enhances the production and diversification of DSCAM variants.
source: Activation of macrophage-like hemocytes in the Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis) enhances the production and diversification of DSCAM variants in both circulating and membrane-bound forms (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: DSCAM that can bind to pathogens is internalized through homodimeric interaction between circulating and membrane-bound forms, activating the adaptor protein Dreadlocks.
source: DSCAM that can bind to pathogens is subsequently internalized through homodimeric interaction between circulating and membrane-bound forms, activating the adaptor protein Dreadlocks (Dock) (Li and Guan, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Guan, 2004 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Dock physically interacts with and activates various serine/threonine kinases, triggering phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of Dorsal and activation of MAPK-ERK-JNK signaling cascade.
source: Dock physically interacts with and activates various serine/threonine kinases, thus triggering signaling events such as phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the NFĸB homolog Dorsal, as well as the activation of MAPK-ERK-JNK signaling cascade.
evidence: This describes the signaling cascade downstream of DSCAM activation, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: DSCAM signaling leads to increased production of antimicrobial peptides and a shift in the ratio of hnRNP (hrp36) and SR-protein (B52).
source: These signals lead to increased production of antimicrobial peptides and a shift in the ratio of hnRNP (hrp36) and SR-protein (B52).
evidence: This describes the downstream effects of DSCAM signaling, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The shift in HRP36 and B52 ratio may stabilize the alternative splicing machinery and limit Dscam splicing to produce only a few preselected DSCAM isoforms.
source: This shift may stabilize the alternative splicing machinery and limit Dscam splicing to produce only a few preselected DSCAM isoforms (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2019 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Dscam signaling activates a disintegrin and metalloproteinase, which sheds the outer DSCAM domains, enabling cleavage of its cytosolic domain by γ-secretase.
source: In addition to stabilizing splicing, Dscam signaling further activates the a disintegrin and metalloproteinase, which sheds the outer DSCAM domains, enabling cleavage of its cytosolic domain by γ-secretase (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2021 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The intracellular domain of DSCAM interacts with importin proteins, which guide it to the nucleus, initiating a program that promotes cell persistence and proliferation.
source: The intracellular domain then interacts with importin proteins, which guide it to the nucleus, initiating a program that promotes cell persistence and proliferation (Xia et al., 2024; Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xia et al., 2024; Ng et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Infection-induced proliferation is commonly observed in many insect species, particularly during larval and pupal stages.
source: Indeed, infection-induced proliferation is commonly observed in many insect species, particularly during larval and pupal stages (Eleftherianos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eleftherianos et al., 2021.

claim: Some insect species with well-documented immune memory display limited proliferative potential in immune cells during the adult stage.
source: However, some insect species with well-documented immune memory display limited proliferative potential in immune cells during the adult stage, and no specific hematopoietic organs or niches have been identified as responsible for immune memory maintenance so far (Sanchez Bosch et al., 2019; Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanchez Bosch et al., 2019; Ghosh et al., 2015.

claim: Dscam mRNA might be stored in various membraneless organelles, such as p-bodies or ω-speckles.
source: Dscam mRNA might be stored in various membraneless organelles, such as p-bodies, or ω-speckles (Luo et al., 2018), consistent with evidence of numerous RNA-binding proteins interacting with Dscam mRNA in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2018.

claim: Drosophila offers unparalleled genetic tools for manipulating the expression of investigated genes.
source: Drosophila offers unparalleled genetic tools for manipulating the expression of investigated genes as well as a broad variety of reporter strains (Tolwinski, 2017; Rajan and Perrimon, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tolwinski, 2017; Rajan and Perrimon, 2011.

claim: The Gal4-UAS system allows researchers to control gene expression in particular cells without affecting other tissues.
source: This system allows researchers to control gene expression in particular cells, such as immune cells, without affecting other tissues.
evidence: This describes the established capabilities of the Gal4-UAS system.

claim: The insect immune system shows many evolutionarily conserved features with the mammalian innate immune system.
source: The insect immune system shows many evolutionarily conserved features with the mammalian innate immune system.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in comparative immunology.

claim: Insects evolved over 400 million years ago.
source: In addition, since insects evolved over 400 million years ago, their ability to 'remember' infections without adaptive immunity suggests that innate immune memory is a fundamental trait that predates the evolution of vertebrate adaptive immune system.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect evolution.

claim: The ability of insects to remember infections without adaptive immunity suggests that innate immune memory is a fundamental trait that predates the evolution of vertebrate adaptive immune system.
source: In addition, since insects evolved over 400 million years ago, their ability to 'remember' infections without adaptive immunity suggests that innate immune memory is a fundamental trait that predates the evolution of vertebrate adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evidence presented.

claim: The formation of innate immune memory involves epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation and histone acetylation.
source: The formation of innate immune memory involves epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation and histone acetylation, which can persist long after an infection has cleared.
evidence: This is based on evidence presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Some studies suggest that immune memory can be passed on to offspring, enabling challenged parents to produce progeny with enhanced immune defenses.
source: Intriguingly, some studies suggest that immune memory can be passed on to offspring, enabling challenged parents to produce progeny with enhanced immune defenses (Gegner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gegner et al., 2019.

claim: Vaccination remains one of the most significant breakthroughs in immunology, saving millions of lives each year.
source: Vaccination remains one of the most significant breakthroughs in immunology, saving millions of lives each year and helping humanity overcome some of the deadliest and most devastating diseases (Riedel, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riedel, 2005.

claim: Injection or feeding of viral nucleic acids alone can provide individuals with a baseline level of acquired immunity against secondary infections.
source: This is supported by preliminary experiments and empirical data, showing that injection or feeding of viral nucleic acids alone can provide individuals with a baseline level of acquired immunity against secondary infections (Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saleh et al., 2009; Tassetto et al., 2017.

claim: In mosquitoes, both feeding and injection of viral RNA increase resistance to secondary viral infections.
source: In mosquitoes, both feeding and injection of viral RNA increase resistance to secondary viral infections, with protective effects observed even after injecting as few as 105 copies of viral RNA (Romoli et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Romoli et al., 2024.

claim: Injection of lipopolysaccharides prior to Metarhizium anisopliae exposure confers protection in Tenebrio molitor.
source: Efficient prophylaxis has been achieved also against entomopathogenic fungi as injection of lipopolysaccharides prior to Metarhizium anisopliae exposure confers protection in T. molitor (Moret and Siva-Jothy, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moret and Siva-Jothy, 2003.

claim: Improved resistance to viral infections has been documented in honeybees fed bacteria heterologously expressing plasmids with viral nucleic acid fragments.
source: An innovative approach has also been developed in honeybees, where improved resistance to viral infections has been documented in individuals fed bacteria heterologously expressing plasmids with viral nucleic acid fragments (Ricigliano et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ricigliano et al., 2024.

claim: Feeding honeybees with attenuated Paenibacillus larvae has proven to be an effective treatment against American foulbrood.
source: Recently, feeding honeybees with attenuated P. larvae has proven to be an effective treatment against American foulbrood (Dickel et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickel et al., 2022.

claim: Honeybee colonies are currently threatened by the widespread transmission of several viral and bacterial pandemic diseases.
source: Honeybee colonies are currently threatened by the widespread transmission of several viral and bacterial pandemic diseases (Parveen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parveen et al., 2022.

claim: Blood-feeding insects transmit a number of diseases that claim millions of victims every year.
source: On the other hand, blood-feeding insects, especially in tropical areas, transmit a number of diseases that claim millions of victims every year (Belluco et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belluco et al., 2023.

claim: Mosquitoes, ticks, tsetse flies, and fleas do not sufficiently suppress the pathogens they carry, making them ideal vectors and reservoirs for pathogen multiplication.
source: The challenge posed by insect vectors of human diseases lies in their high tolerance to human pathogens. Mosquitoes, ticks, tsetse flies, and fleas do not sufficiently suppress the pathogens they carry, making them not only ideal vectors but also reservoirs for pathogen multiplication.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about insect disease vectors.

claim: Manipulating the immune tolerance of insect vectors to the pathogens they transmit is a currently considered strategy to reduce pathogen spread.
source: Manipulating the immune tolerance of these vectors to the pathogens they transmit is a currently considered strategy to reduce pathogen spread and, consequently, the incidence of the diseases they cause (Lambrechts and Saleh, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lambrechts and Saleh, 2019.
